## Introduction

The **continuous uniform distribution** is a continuous probability
distribution in which all outcomes in a bounded interval are equally
likely. It is the simplest continuous distribution and the continuous
analogue of the [[discrete-uniform-distribution]].

:::{.definition data-title="Continuous Uniform Distribution"}

A random variable $X$ follows a **continuous uniform distribution** on
the interval $[a, b]$ with $a < b$ if

$$
X \sim \text{Uniform}(a, b) \quad \text{or}
  \quad X \sim U(a, b).
$$

:::

The most common case is the **standard uniform distribution** on $[0, 1]$,
denoted $U(0, 1)$.

## Probability Density Function

:::{.definition data-title="Probability Density Function (PDF)"}

The probability density function is

$$
f(x) = \begin{cases}
  \dfrac{1}{b - a} & x \in [a, b], \\[4pt]
  0 & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
$$

:::

*Interpretation:* The constant value $\frac{1}{b-a}$ ensures that the
density integrates to $1$ over $[a, b]$; no value in the interval is
preferred over any other.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Plotting code"
#| fig-cap: "Density of the standard uniform $U(0, 1)$."
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

sns.set_style('whitegrid')
sns.set_palette('Set2')

a, b = 0.0, 1.0
x = np.linspace(a - 0.5, b + 0.5, 500)
y = np.where((x >= a) & (x <= b), 1 / (b - a), 0.0)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.plot(x, y, color='#4c72b0', lw=2)
ax.fill_between(x, y, color='#4c72b0', alpha=0.2)
ax.axvline((a + b) / 2, color='#c44e52', ls='--', lw=1.5,
           label=r'$\mathbb{E}[X]$')

ax.set_xlabel('$x$')
ax.set_ylabel('$f(x)$')
ax.set_title(r'Uniform density $U(0,\ 1)$')
ax.set_ylim(0, 1.4)
ax.legend()
plt.show()
```

:::{.definition data-title="Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF)"}

The cumulative distribution function is

$$
F(x) = \begin{cases}
  0 & x < a, \\[2pt]
  \dfrac{x - a}{b - a} & a \leq x \leq b, \\[4pt]
  1 & x > b.
\end{cases}
$$

:::

## Key Properties

:::{.theorem data-title="Moments of the Uniform Distribution"}

The expectation and variance of $X \sim \text{Uniform}(a, b)$ are

$$
\mathbb{E}[X] = \frac{a + b}{2} \quad \& \quad
  \operatorname{Var}(X) = \frac{(b - a)^2}{12}.
$$

:::

:::{.proof}

Directly,

$$
\mathbb{E}[X] = \int_a^b \frac{x}{b - a} \, dx
  = \frac{b^2 - a^2}{2(b - a)} = \frac{a + b}{2}.
$$

Since $\mathbb{E}[X^2] = \frac{a^2 + ab + b^2}{3}$,

$$
\operatorname{Var}(X) = \frac{a^2 + ab + b^2}{3}
  - \frac{(a + b)^2}{4} = \frac{(b - a)^2}{12}.
$$

:::

## Generating Functions

:::{.theorem data-title="Moment Generating Function"}

The **moment generating function (MGF)** of
$X \sim \text{Uniform}(a, b)$ is

$$
M_X(t) = \frac{e^{tb} - e^{ta}}{t(b - a)},
  \quad t \neq 0,
$$

with $M_X(0) = 1$.

:::

:::{.theorem data-title="Characteristic Function"}

The characteristic function of $X \sim \text{Uniform}(a, b)$ is

$$
\varphi_X(t) = \frac{e^{itb} - e^{ita}}{it(b - a)},
  \quad t \neq 0.
$$

:::

## Affine Transformations and Order Statistics

:::{.theorem data-title="Linear Transformation"}

If $X \sim \text{Uniform}(a, b)$ and $Y = cX + d$ with $c > 0$, then

$$
Y \sim \text{Uniform}(ca + d, cb + d).
$$

In particular, if $X \sim U(0, 1)$ then $(b - a)X + a \sim U(a, b)$.

:::

:::{.theorem data-title="Order Statistics"}

If $U_1, \ldots, U_n$ are i.i.d. $U(0, 1)$ with order statistics
$U_{(1)} \leq \cdots \leq U_{(n)}$, then the $k$-th order statistic
follows a [[beta-distribution]]:

$$
U_{(k)} \sim \text{Beta}(k, n + 1 - k).
$$

:::

## Relationship to Other Distributions

- **[[discrete-uniform-distribution]]:** The discrete analogue on a finite
  set of equally likely values.
- **[[beta-distribution]]:** $U(0, 1) = \text{Beta}(1, 1)$, and order
  statistics of uniforms are Beta distributed.
- **Inverse transform sampling:** If $F$ is a continuous CDF and
  $U \sim U(0, 1)$, then $F^{-1}(U)$ has distribution $F$ — the basis for
  simulating any [[random-variable-transformations]].

## Examples and Applications

:::{.example data-title="Random number generation"}

$U(0, 1)$ is the foundation for generating samples from any distribution
via inverse transform sampling.

:::

:::{.example data-title="Arrival within a window"}

If an event is equally likely to occur at any time in a fixed window, its
arrival time is modelled as $\text{Uniform}(a, b)$.

:::

:::{.example data-title="Tolerances"}

A measurement known only to lie within a specified tolerance band, with
no further information, is often modelled as uniform over that band.

:::
